reasoning: The proposal's core observation — that a monitor's benign suspicion distribution and thus FPR vary by domain, so a single fixed audit threshold silently mis-calibrates per-domain and changes detection rates — is explicitly recognized in published AI-control work. The "Monitoring benchmark for AI control" states TPR-at-1%-FPR "requires a separate threshold for each dataset which is generally unrealistic for practical monitoring setups," directly articulating the per-domain threshold mismatch; "Practical challenges of control monitoring in frontier AI deployments" (arXiv 2512.22154, Dec 2025) treats calibration under heterogeneous real deployments; and per-domain FPR variation is empirically documented (5-9% across scientific domains; strong category dependence of violation/flag rates by task type in BashArena/Async Control). What remains genuinely unexplored is the proposal's specific framing as a standalone empirical study isolating benign-distribution drift across innocuous everyday domains (coding/web/email/file management) and quantifying the resulting detection-rate divergence at a fixed audit budget — prior work flags the effect in passing rather than measuring it as the central contribution. Hence the problem is largely addressed conceptually, with a minor methodological gap in dedicated quantification.

evidence.title: Monitoring benchmark for AI control
evidence.summary: Reports TPR at 1% FPR on a per-dataset basis and explicitly notes this 'requires a separate threshold for each dataset which is generally unrealistic for practical monitoring setups' — directly stating the proposal's core insight that per-domain calibration differs from a single practical fixed threshold. Also notes the 99th-percentile-of-honest-runs threshold and that the benign 99th-percentile suspicion score varies by agent model.

evidence.title: Practical challenges of control monitoring in frontier AI deployments (2512.22154)
evidence.summary: Dec 2025 paper analyzing how scaling trusted monitoring to real heterogeneous deployments breaks simplifying assumptions, including FPR-budget calibration (auditors review only ~2% of traffic so monitors must be calibrated to that FPR) across diverse deployment conditions — covering the calibration-under-shift problem the proposal targets.

evidence.title: BashArena / Async Control: per-task-category violation and flag-rate dependence
evidence.summary: Documents pronounced category dependence in agent/monitor behavior across task types (e.g., research/communication vs sysadmin tasks show very different violation rates), evidence that benign and flagged-score distributions shift substantially across domains, undermining a single global threshold.

evidence.title: Domain-dependent monitor false positive rates
evidence.summary: Empirical reports that domain detectors show FPR variation (e.g., 5-9% across Chemistry/Biology/Physics), and that false positive rates vary significantly across domains due to differing inherent task characteristics — directly supporting the claim that a fixed threshold yields divergent FPR per domain.

evidence.title: Online Shift Detection and Conformal Adaptation for Deployed Safety Classifiers (2606.11949)
evidence.summary: Proposes online monitors that detect when a deployed safety classifier's score distribution moves out of distribution and adapt thresholds, showing the calibration-drift-under-distribution-shift problem for safety monitors is already an active, methodologically developed research area (going beyond mere measurement to adaptive correction).
